opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the most interesting part started before the prover touched anything: the formalization step. When a Putnam problem comes out, it's written in natural language for human contestants, and to have Axiom Prover work on it in Lean, you first need a faithful formal statement. That's harder than people expect. A word like "find all" or "determine the value" doesn't map cleanly onto a theorem statement, because in Lean you can't just say "find the answer." You have to commit to a candidate answer and then prove it's correct, and you have to make sure you haven't accidentally made the problem easier or subtly different. Getting the statement exactly right, with no loopholes and nothing lost, takes real mathematical care.

The second thing that struck me was how differently the problems felt to a machine than to a human. Some problems a strong undergraduate would call routine, a bit of algebra and a clean inequality, turned out to be painful formally, because the "obvious" steps humans skip have to be spelled out, and the library support for a particular corner of analysis or combinatorics might be thin. Other problems that humans find tricky, where the key is one clever insight, were sometimes more tractable for the system once it found the right lemma, because after that the verification is mechanical.

The third thing, which I find the most meaningful, is what a formal proof gives you. When a language model writes a natural-language Putnam solution, someone still has to grade it, and graders can disagree or miss a gap. When Lean accepts a proof, there's no ambiguity. It's checked down to the axioms. So for us the competition wasn't just about the score. It was a demonstration that you can get to a world where mathematical reasoning from an AI is verifiable by construction, not by trust.

And on a personal level, I competed in math olympiads growing up, so seeing a system work through problems from a contest I have a lot of affection for, and occasionally find a proof route different from the one a human would naturally take, was both humbling and exciting. It made me think the interesting future isn't AI replacing mathematicians. It's AI giving mathematicians a collaborator whose work they can fully trust.

r002.rationale: It says the system sometimes found a proof route different from the one a human would naturally take.

fable-5.1.text:
What was interesting to me was that the hard part wasn't the math itself, it was the translation. The Putnam problems come out as natural language on a Saturday morning, and before Axiom Prover can touch them, somebody has to turn each one into a formal statement in Lean. That sounds mechanical, but it's actually where a lot of subtle judgment lives.

Take a problem that says "find all functions such that..." or "determine the smallest constant for which..." A human reads that and understands it's really two problems: guess the answer, then prove it's right. In Lean you have to decide what you're committing to. Do you formalize it with the answer filled in, so the prover only has to verify? Or do you leave the answer as an unknown and ask the system to discover it? We wanted the latter wherever we could, because that's the honest version of the competition, but it makes the formal statement much more delicate. You have to make sure you haven't accidentally made the problem trivial or, worse, false.

We had a strict rule about doing this quickly and without peeking at any solutions, because the whole point was to show what the system could do under real conditions. So the human team was formalizing under time pressure while the model was already starting to work, and there's a bit of tension there. If you write a slightly wrong statement, the prover will happily prove the wrong thing, and Lean will check it, and you'll feel great until someone points out the statement didn't capture the problem. We caught one or two of those in review, and that was a good reminder that formal verification guarantees the proof, not the question.

The other thing that surprised me was watching which problems were hard for the system versus hard for humans. Some of the problems that top students find scary, with lots of casework, were fine for Axiom because it doesn't get bored or sloppy. And a couple that humans find almost routine took much longer, usually because the natural proof relies on a picture or an intuition that doesn't have a clean library lemma behind it yet. So preparing the problems also taught us a lot about where the gaps are in the formal math ecosystem, and that's honestly what we care about long term, more than the score on any one competition.

r001.rationale: The response says humans could fill in an answer or leave it unknown, and that they preferred leaving it unknown where possible. It does not say the team had to determine the answer themselves.

r002.rationale: The response compares which problems were difficult for Axiom and for humans, but does not report that Axiom’s eventual approaches to solving the problems differed from the mathematicians’ approaches.

astra-6.text:
What I found interesting was the gap between a problem as a human reads it and a problem stated precisely enough for a theorem prover. With a Putnam problem, a mathematician brings a lot of implicit understanding—what the notation means, what assumptions are in play, which facts can be taken for granted. Preparing it for Axiom Prover means making that explicit without accidentally changing the problem or giving away the solution.

And that raises a really interesting question: how much of the difficulty is finding the mathematical insight, and how much is expressing and verifying that insight? Those are closely connected, but they’re not quite the same thing.

sol-6.1.text:
What I found interesting was the gap between a problem as a human reads it and a problem stated precisely enough for a prover. On paper, you can leave a lot implicit: what the variables range over, which assumptions matter, even what counts as a complete answer. Preparing a problem forces you to make those choices explicit.

And you have to be careful that you’re clarifying the question without giving away the solution. You want Axiom Prover to do the mathematical work, so choosing the right representation is itself an interesting challenge. It makes you think about where understanding the statement ends and solving the problem begins.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare Axiom Prover’s eventual approaches with the human mathematicians’ approaches.
